interactions.label: HIV encodes its genome as double-stranded DNA.

params.question: HIV encodes its genome as double-stranded DNA.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: HIV carries two copies of single-stranded RNA as its genome. As a retrovirus, it uses reverse transcriptase to convert RNA into proviral DNA — the reverse of the normal transcription direction. This is why the family is called Retroviridae.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. HIV is a retrovirus that carries two copies of single-stranded RNA, not DNA. It uses reverse transcriptase to convert this RNA into proviral DNA after entering the host cell.

interactions.label: During clinical latency (phase 2), a person with HIV appears healthy for 8–10 ye

params.question: During clinical latency (phase 2), a person with HIV appears healthy for 8–10 years. What is happening to the CD4+ T-cell count during this period?

answers.text: It remains stable at the pre-infection level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The CD4 count does not remain stable. HIV continues to replicate at low levels even during latency, steadily destroying CD4+ T cells over years.

answers.text: It gradually declines from approximately 1,000 to around 200 cells/μL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. During clinical latency, HIV silently replicates and progressively destroys CD4+ T cells. The count drops from ~1,000 to ~200 over 8–10 years, after which AIDS develops.

answers.text: It drops sharply at infection and stays below 200 cells/μL throughout

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sharp drop occurs during the acute phase (phase 1), not latency. During latency, the count partially recovers after the acute dip and then declines gradually over years.

answers.text: It rises due to compensatory immune activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although the immune system mounts a partial response during latency, it cannot keep pace with ongoing viral destruction. The net effect is a slow, steady CD4 decline.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three phases of HIV infection. During latency, the virus replicates silently, causing a slow but relentless decline in CD4+ T cells from ~1,000 to ~200 over 8–10 years.
Exactly right. The gradual CD4 decline during latency explains why patients feel well for years before AIDS manifests.

params.question: A patient with HIV and active tuberculosis begins antiretroviral therapy. Four weeks later, fever worsens and cervical lymph nodes enlarge, despite a declining viral load and rising CD4 count. What is the most likely explanation?

answers.text: The antiretroviral drugs are ineffective due to viral resistance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Drug resistance would be reflected in a rising or persistently high viral load. Here the viral load is declining, indicating the drugs are working against HIV.

answers.text: A new, unrelated opportunistic infection has developed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: With a rising CD4 count and falling viral load, the immune system is recovering. New opportunistic infections are less likely in this setting; the pattern points to inflammation against an existing pathogen.

Correct. IRIS occurs when the recovering immune system mounts vigorous inflammation against a pre-existing pathogen such as TB. It typically appears 4–8 weeks after starting ART and must not be mistaken for treatment failure.

answers.text: An adverse drug reaction to the antiretroviral regimen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Drug reactions can cause fever, but the localised lymph node enlargement alongside improving HIV markers specifically suggests an immune-mediated response to the existing TB — characteristic of IRIS.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a patient worsens after starting ART despite improving viral load and CD4 count, think of IRIS — the recovering immune system attacking a pre-existing pathogen. This is not treatment failure.
Well analysed. Recognising IRIS prevents the mistake of stopping effective antiretroviral therapy when the patient actually needs continued treatment.

interactions.label: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a confirmed HIV-positive

params.question: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a confirmed HIV-positive patient. Which post-exposure prophylaxis regimen should be initiated, and within what time frame?

answers.text: Tenofovir + emtricitabine daily, beginning within 7 days of exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tenofovir + emtricitabine is the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) combination for ongoing prevention in high-risk individuals, not the post-exposure regimen. PEP requires a three-drug regimen and a much shorter initiation window.

answers.text: Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir for 28 days, within 72 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) uses three drugs — tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir — for 28 days. It must be started within 72 hours of exposure to be effective.

answers.text: Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir for 7 days, within 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the drug combination is correct, PEP requires a full 28-day course, not 7 days. The initiation window is 72 hours, not 24 hours.
This two-drug combination is used for PrEP, not PEP. Post-exposure prophylaxis requires a three-drug regimen including dolutegravir to maximise the chance of preventing infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: PEP uses tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir for 28 days and must start within 72 hours. Do not confuse it with PrEP (tenofovir + emtricitabine daily for ongoing prevention).
Correct. Remembering the PEP regimen — tenofovir, lamivudine, dolutegravir for 28 days within 72 hours — and distinguishing it from PrEP is essential for clinical practice.
